title: The Aztec gods and human sacrifice
subtitle: Blood for the sun
subject: mythologie
description: For the Aztecs, the sun rises only if the gods are given blood. A harsh but coherent cosmology, right at the heart of their empire.

hero.hook: Without blood the sun would stop: such is the cosmic debt of the Aztecs.

blocks.text: The **Aztecs**, or Mexica, believed the universe was fragile. The gods needed blood for the sun to keep moving. Without offerings, chaos would come back.
What horrified the Spanish rests on one clear idea: the life of the gods and the life of human beings are tied together. Here is how that cosmology works.

sections.title: The Five Suns: a world that has already died four times

blocks.text: In the myth of the [[Five Suns]], four ages have already ended in disaster. Ours is the fifth sun, [[Nahui Ollin]] (“4-Movement”), and it is fated to end in earthquakes.

blocks.caption: The Sun Stone: Aztec time turns through one era after another

blocks.text: At **Teotihuacán**, the sacred city of the central plateau, the gods throw themselves into a fire to become sun and moon. But the sun stays still. The other gods then offer their own blood to set it moving. Human beings inherit that debt.
For the Aztecs, sacrifice was not cruelty for its own sake: it was the repayment of a divine debt, the [[cosmology of the Five Suns and the cosmic debt]].

The central god is [[Huitzilopochtli]], god of war and of the noon sun. Every night he fights the darkness so he can be reborn in the morning. Beside him, [[Tlaloc]] hands out rain, and with it the harvest, or famine.

blocks.caption: Huitzilopochtli, the warrior sun who demands to be fed

blocks.text: [[Quetzalcoatl]], the Feathered Serpent, stands for knowledge and civilization. His rival [[Tezcatlipoca]], the Smoking Mirror, rules the night, fate and magic. The earth itself has a terrible face: [[Coatlicue]], the devouring mother goddess.
The precious blood offered to the gods is called [[chalchihuatl]], “precious water.” The heart cut from the body is imagined as a spark of sun handed back to the sky.
To obtain victims, the Aztecs staged the [[Xochiyaoyotl]], the “flower wars”: ritual battles whose aim was not to kill but to capture living warriors worthy of being offered.

blocks.caption: Sacrifice at the top of the temple: the heart held up to the sun

blocks.text: At the top of the **Templo Mayor** in Tenochtitlán, the capital built on a lake, a priest cut out the heart with an **obsidian** knife, a razor-sharp volcanic stone. The act was public and solemn, understood as a service rendered to the sun.

events.title: Sacrifice of the gods
events.detail: The sun receives divine blood so it can move.

sections.title: The end of a world, lasting traces

blocks.text: Spanish chronicles sometimes inflated the figures to justify the conquest. But the sacrificial system was real enough. In **1519**, the arrival of **Hernán Cortés** brought this ritual world to a sudden end.

Even so, Aztec figures survive in a blended religion: the Virgin of Guadalupe appeared on a site once linked to a mother goddess. To understand these sacrifices is to understand a culture that put the survival of the cosmos above the individual.
For the Aztecs, human blood fed the sun. The gods had already paid with their lives, so people repaid that debt through sacrifice, above all through the **flower wars**.
